title: Bhaja Govindam
hookLine: the great philosopher of not-two hears an old man cramming grammar, and bursts into song
carry: knowledge and devotion meet in the end
tomorrow: what if the soul and God stay two, forever?
last: THE ONE WHO NOTICES ALL FIVE.

cards: Varanasi, in a story people tell about Shankara. He's walking with his students and passes an old man, gray-haired, bent over a book, reciting Sanskrit grammar rules.
Over and over, drilling them, as if his life depended on it. Shankara stops. No argument, no lecture on not two.
The philosopher sings. A song that begins: worship Govinda, worship Govinda, worship Govinda, foolish mind. When the end comes, grammar rules won't save you.

teach.b: The song is called Bhaja Govindam, and people still sing it today. Tradition credits it to Shankara, with verses added by his students.
It's playful and sharp: a whole life spent chasing money, status and cleverness, and the refrain keeps breaking in, worship Govinda. That surprises people. The teacher of not two, singing to Krishna?
But this is a real Hindu teaching: in the Advaita tradition, devotion and knowledge aren't enemies.
Advaita teachers often put it this way: devotion purifies the mind so it can see clearly, and the deepest devotion and the deepest knowledge meet at the same place.
Monasteries of Shankara's line, such as Sringeri, keep temple worship and hymns alongside study. A well-known line, often credited to Shankara, sums up the school in half a breath.
Paraphrased: Brahman is real. The world is mithya, dependent reality.

teach.h: THE SELF, NOT OTHER THAN BRAHMAN.
teach.b: And the self is not other than Brahman. That's the week. The pots and the clay: one stuff, many names.
The rope and the snake: separation borrowed, and a lamp, not a stick. Narada's water, and maya: real while it lasts. The boy and the crocodile, and three rare things.
The student burning, and the teacher saying: don't be afraid. Bhrigu's five sheaths, and the one who sees them. And an old man at his grammar, and a song.
Tomorrow, the teachers who looked at the same Upanishads and said: no. The soul and God stay two, and that's not a problem. It's the whole point.
Both views are alive today. Neither is ranked here.

how: Bhaja Govindam, traditionally credited to Shankara, is widely sung and recited; in Advaita monasteries such as Sringeri, study of non-duality goes together with temple worship and devotional hymns.

o: a school that rejects all worship and hymns
not two: the self is not other than Brahman
two: the self and God, separate forever

games.q: the week of Advaita — tap the pairs.

s: Shankara is credited with devotional hymns, and his line still leads temple worship.
Bhaja Govindam is still widely sung
tradition credits it to Shankara, with verses by his students.
this course treats Advaita as the correct Hindu view

games.q: you're Shankara in Varanasi. an old man is cramming grammar rules as if his life depended on it. what does the story say you do?
games.why: he sings Bhaja Govindam: worship Govinda, foolish mind; when the end comes, grammar rules won't save you.

practice: Let the week's pictures pass, one per breath: the clay, the rope, Narada's water, the crocodile, don't be afraid, the five sheaths.
Then ask the question the old man with the grammar book forgot, and don't answer quickly: what am I spending my days drilling, and does it matter at the end?
If you pray, let a name of God rise, the way Shankara sang; if not, rest in the question.

wordCard.voice: Advaita, Shankara's school of not two: Brahman is real, the world is dependent, and the self is not other than Brahman. And its great philosopher also sang: worship Govinda.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bhaja govindam, 'worship Govinda' (Krishna); bhaja is from bhaj, the root of bhakti.

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge and devotion meet in the end. The philosopher of not two still sang. See you tomorrow.
